title: A Public Official May Not Authorize Disclosure He Knows to Be False: $1.3 Billion and a 21(a) Report

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The money was raised from the public market on documents the Commission found defective: "Six of these municipal offerings by the County collectively raised approximately $1.3 billion and are the subject of this report."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the dependence of the securities on the pools. The report sets out four ways the offerings were tied to the County Pools — proceeds reinvested in them for interest earnings, funds pledged to repay securities invested in them, the Pools agreeing to repurchase or repay certain securities, and "the County’s economic reliance on the County Pools materially affected its ability to repay the securities."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was in the Official Statements, and the finding is flat: they "contained material misstatements and omissions concerning the risks relating to, among other things, the County Pools and the financial condition of Orange County, including its ability to repay the securities."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the omissions preserved was continued market access on terms that did not price the risk — six offerings over 1993 and 1994, the period the investigation covers, raising approximately $1.3 billion from investors who were not told what the report says they should have been told.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The disposition is the interesting part and it is a choice the Commission explains. Against the officers, action: a settled civil injunctive action against the former Treasurer-Tax Collector and the former Assistant Treasurer, enjoining future antifraud violations, and a settled cease and desist proceeding against the County, the Flood Control District and the Board of Supervisors. Against the individual Supervisors, no charges — instead a Section 21(a) report "to emphasize the responsibilities under the federal securities laws of local government officials who authorize the issuance of municipal securities". A report that states a duty in place of charging the people who owed it.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A municipal securities market in which the issuer is primarily liable for its own disclosure and no regulator reviews an Official Statement before it is used.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The duty this report announces for public officials personally: "a public official may not authorize disclosure that the official knows to be false", applied to those "who have ultimate authority to approve the issuance of securities and related disclosure documents".
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The pools’ reported earnings supported the county’s finances; the county’s finances supported the offerings; the offerings fed proceeds back into the pools. Each leg depended on the others being described accurately, and the report found they were not.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That one county treasurer gambled on exotic derivatives and bankrupted Orange County while the elected board knew nothing about it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission did act against the treasurer and his assistant — both were enjoined from future antifraud violations by settled civil action. But it declined the knew-nothing framing for the board, and it said so by issuing a Section 21(a) report specifically "in the Matter of County of Orange, California as it Relates to the Conduct of the Members of the Board of Supervisors", addressed to "the conduct of the individual members of the Board of Supervisors ... in authorizing the issuance of these municipal securities". It also settled a cease and desist proceeding against the Board of Supervisors as a body. The report's stated purpose is to set out what officials who authorise offerings are responsible for. What should not be read into it is a finding of individual liability: a 21(a) report states the Commission's views and charges no one, the Supervisors were not charged, and the Commission recorded that its investigation was ongoing.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An SEC Report of Investigation under Section 21(a), Exchange Act Release No. 36761, dated 24 January 1996, into events of 1993 and 1994. Six County offerings raising approximately $1.3 billion. Official Statements containing material misstatements and omissions about the County Pools and the County’s financial condition and its ability to repay. Four specified links between the securities and the pools. A settled civil injunctive action against former Treasurer-Tax Collector Robert L. Citron and former Assistant Treasurer Matthew R. Raabe. A settled cease and desist proceeding against the County, the Flood Control District and the Board of Supervisors. No charges against individual Supervisors, and instead a published statement of the duty: public entities "are primarily liable for the content of their disclosure documents", and an official with ultimate authority to approve them "may not authorize disclosure that the official knows to be false".

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Report of Investigation in the Matter of County of Orange, California as it Relates to the Conduct of the Members of the Board of Supervisors, Exchange Act Release No. 36761 (24 January 1996), Section 21(a) of the Exchange Act
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from sec.gov, where the full text of the Section 21(a) report is published on the Commission's "Municipal Bond Participants: Public Officials and Obligated Persons" page. (The page is a collection of reports of investigation; the Orange County report is reproduced on it in full and is what is cited here.) THE SUBJECT: "The staff of the Division of Enforcement has conducted an investigation into various events in 1993 and 1994 involving material misrepresentations and omissions in connection with the offer and sale of certain municipal securities, including those issued by the County of Orange, California ... Six of these municipal offerings by the County collectively raised approximately $1.3 billion and are the subject of this report." THE FINDING ON THE DOCUMENTS: "The Official Statements for these municipal securities offerings contained material misstatements and omissions concerning the risks relating to, among other things, the County Pools and the financial condition of Orange County, including its ability to repay the securities." WHAT ELSE THE COMMISSION DID THE SAME DAY: it "filed and settled a related civil injunctive action against the former County Treasurer-Tax Collector, Robert L. Citron ... and the former Assistant Treasurer, Matthew R. Raabe ... pursuant to which they will be enjoined from future violations of the antifraud provisions", and "instituted and settled a related cease and desist proceeding ... against Orange County, the Orange County Flood Control District and the Board of Supervisors of Orange County". THE POINT OF ISSUING A 21(a) REPORT RATHER THAN CHARGING THE SUPERVISORS, stated by the Commission: it is "issuing this Report to emphasize the responsibilities under the federal securities laws of local government officials who authorize the issuance of municipal securities and related disclosure documents and the critical role such officials play with respect to the representations contained in the Official Statements for those securities." And the standard it sets out: "Public entities that issue securities are primarily liable for the content of their disclosure documents"; and "public officials of the issuer who have ultimate authority to approve the issuance of securities and related disclosure documents have responsibilities under the federal securities laws as well. In authorizing the issuance of securities and related disclosure documents, a public official may not authorize disclosure that the official knows to be false". The report records that "The Commission's investigation is ongoing" as at its date. A Section 21(a) report states the Commission's views; it is not an adjudication and it charges no one.
